Chapter Eight: Activism, Allyship, and the Courage to Speak Up
You know, there comes a time when just learning isn’t enough—when you feel that urge to actually do something. For some people, activism is bold and loud: they’re out there marching, holding signs, chanting for change.
But for others, it’s a little quieter, isn’t it? Maybe it’s calling out a sexist comment at work, or being there for a friend who’s going through a tough patch. Sometimes, it’s as simple as donating to a group that’s fighting for justice.
Picture this: someone remembers the very first time they spoke up in a meeting, challenging a policy that was unfair to women. The room went totally silent. For a second, they wondered, “Did I just mess up?”
But after the meeting, a colleague pulled them aside and said, “Thank you. I’ve wanted to say something for months.” That moment proved that courage is contagious. One brave voice can make it easier for others to speak up, too.
Here’s something to pay attention to—activism isn’t about being perfect, or having all the answers. It’s about showing up, even if it feels awkward or uncomfortable. It’s about using the power and privilege you have, in whatever way you can, to make things a little more fair.
Most of us don’t realize how much impact those small acts can really have. Maybe it’s writing a letter to your local official, having an honest conversation with a neighbor, or even sharing something meaningful on social media.
Now, allyship is a huge part of this. It’s about listening to people whose experiences are different from yours, and making sure their voices are heard rather than drowned out. Sometimes, it means admitting when you’ve made a mistake, apologizing, and trying again.
Real allyship isn’t just about being supportive in your head—it’s about action. It’s about standing up, not just standing by.
Think about this story: after learning about intersectionality, someone realized their feminism had always centered their own experience. So, they started seeking out voices from backgrounds different than theirs, went to events led by women of color, and supported causes that didn’t affect them personally.
It wasn’t always easy—sometimes, it was humbling or uncomfortable. But in the end, it was deeply rewarding. They saw that the fight for justice goes way beyond just one person or one group.
The thing is, it’s so easy to stay quiet, to let things slide just to keep the peace. But that silence? It’s its own kind of complicity. The courage to speak up—even in small ways—can send ripples outwards, sparking change in ways we can’t always predict.
So, here’s the key takeaway: activism isn’t some finish line you cross. It’s a practice. It’s about showing up, again and again, even when it feels like progress is slow. It’s about believing that a better world is possible, and being willing to work for it.
